title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Launches Oscar Push for Best Picture, Supporting Actress, and More Categories
body:
The documentary “You Can See Everything,” directed by Nathan Fielder, has officially entered the Oscar race, filing campaigns for Best Picture, Best Supporting Actress, and several technical categories. The move marks an unusual strategy for a nonfiction film that blends investigative journalism with a stylized, almost satirical aesthetic, and it could reshape expectations for how documentaries are positioned during awards season. While the film’s push for Academy honors is clear, its prospects at other major ceremonies—such as the Golden Globes, BAFTAs, and Critics’ Choice—remain uncertain, leaving industry watchers to speculate on how the hybrid work will be received across the broader awards landscape.

The film, which chronicles the rise and fall of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, diverges from traditional documentary storytelling by employing a narrative structure reminiscent of a thriller. Fielder, known for his dead‑pan comedy, assembles a cast of reenactors, archival footage, and a meticulously crafted visual language that blurs the line between fact and performance. This approach has already sparked debate among critics: some praise its inventive form as a fresh way to engage audiences with a well‑trodden cautionary tale, while others worry the stylization may dilute the gravity of Holmes’s alleged fraud. The Oscar campaign leans heavily on the film’s artistic ambition, positioning it as a contender not just for documentary categories but for the top honors usually reserved for narrative features.

Industry insiders note that the decision to vie for Best Picture is especially bold. Historically, only a handful of documentaries—most notably “American Sniper” (though technically a drama) and “Flee”—have broken into the Best Picture conversation, and even then they faced steep odds. “You Can See Everything” hopes to capitalize on the Academy’s recent openness to genre‑bending works, a trend evidenced by the nominations of “The Banshees of Inisherin” and “Everything Everywhere All at Once.” By also submitting for Best Supporting Actress, the campaign highlights the performance of actress (insert name), who portrays a key figure in Holmes’s inner circle. Her nuanced portrayal, which oscillates between empathy and manipulation, has already garnered praise on the festival circuit, suggesting that the film may find a foothold in acting categories where documentaries are rarely represented.

The technical nominations being pursued—such as cinematography, editing, and original score—reflect the film’s production values. Shot largely on location in Silicon Valley and supplemented with recreated office sets, the visual composition employs a muted palette that mirrors the corporate aesthetic of the early 2000s tech boom. The editing, praised for its tight pacing and rhythmic intercutting of courtroom testimony with behind‑the‑scenes footage, underscores the narrative’s tension. Composer (insert name) provides a score that fuses minimalist electronic motifs with orchestral swells, further blurring the line between documentary realism and cinematic drama. These elements could resonate with Academy voters who have increasingly rewarded craftsmanship in non‑fiction works.

However, the campaign’s ambiguity regarding other awards could be a double‑edged sword. The Golden Globes, for instance, separate drama and musical/comedy categories, and their voting body often favors more conventional storytelling. The BAFTAs and Critics’ Choice tend to align more closely with the Academy’s tastes, yet they also weigh the cultural impact of a film within its national context. “You Can See Everything” may find allies among those who view the Theranos saga as a cautionary emblem of American tech hubris, but it must also contend with a crowded field of documentaries tackling social and political issues this season. The lack of a clear strategy for these platforms may limit the film’s momentum beyond the Oscars.

As the awards calendar advances, the documentary’s performance at upcoming festivals and limited‑release screenings will be crucial. Positive word‑of‑mouth could amplify its Oscar campaign, while any criticism of its hybrid form may dampen enthusiasm among voters still wary of genre‑blurring. If “You Can See Everything” manages to secure nominations—or even wins—in the categories it has targeted, it could signal a shift in how the Academy evaluates nonfiction storytelling, encouraging more filmmakers to experiment with narrative techniques. Regardless of the outcome, the film’s bold entry into the Oscar conversation underscores a growing appetite for innovative documentary cinema, and it sets the stage for a potentially transformative awards season.
